title: Advanced prompting techniques

objectives: Use few-shot examples, constraints and step-by-step instructions to improve results
Request structured outputs such as tables and checklists
Use self-critique loops to raise quality
Build a personal prompt playbook with tested prompts
content.intro: In the Beginner path you learned to write clear prompts. At this level you learn to engineer them: to get the same good result every time, in the format you need, for work that other people will rely on. Today you collect a toolbox of techniques and test them on real tasks from your own life or business.

concepts.heading: Examples teach better than descriptions
concepts.text: Showing the AI one to three examples of the output you want is called few-shot prompting, and it is often more powerful than a long explanation. Paste an example of a perfect product description, a perfect reply to an angry customer, or a perfect summary, and say 'write the next one in exactly this style'. Use examples that are typical of your real work, and vary them slightly so the AI learns the pattern and not the exact words.

concepts.heading: Constraints and structure
concepts.text: Constraints stop the AI from wandering: word limits, forbidden words, required sections, reading level, and the order of information. Ask for structure that you can scan or paste into other tools, such as a table with named columns, a checklist, numbered steps or labelled sections. Structured answers are easier to check, easier to reuse and easier to automate later in the course.
points: Length, tone, required sections, banned words
Structure makes checking and automation easier

concepts.heading: Step-by-step and self-critique
concepts.text: For harder tasks ask the AI to work in stages: first list the key points, then draft, then check the draft against a list of requirements and fix any problems. A self-critique prompt such as 'review your answer against these five criteria, score each from 1 to 5 and rewrite anything below 4' often lifts quality noticeably. It does not replace your own review, but it catches many obvious weaknesses before you see them.
points: Ask the AI to score its own draft against criteria

concepts.heading: Testing and recording what works
concepts.text: Professionals test prompts instead of trusting a lucky result. Run the same prompt three times and with two different inputs; if the results vary wildly, tighten the instructions. Compare two prompt versions side by side and keep the better one. Record the winning prompt, the date, what it is for and a sample of good output in your playbook. A playbook of fifteen tested prompts is a real business asset.

steps: Choose five real tasks (a reply, a summary, a product description, a plan, an announcement) and write your current prompt for each
Rewrite each prompt with examples, constraints and a required structure
Run old and new versions side by side and score both from 1 to 5 on accuracy, tone and usefulness
Add a self-critique step to the two weakest results and re-score
Test the best three prompts twice more with different inputs to check consistency
Record your winners in the Prompt Playbook table
content.lab: Take 5 weak real tasks and build high-performance prompts. Run A/B comparison on 2 assistants.

examples.label: Few-shot prompt
examples.text: Here are two examples of good replies to customer complaints: [example 1] [example 2]. Write a reply to this new complaint in exactly the same style: [complaint].

examples.label: Self-critique prompt
examples.text: Review your answer against these criteria: accurate, friendly, under 100 words, one clear next step. Score each from 1 to 5, then rewrite anything below 4.

content.code:
PROMPT PLAYBOOK ENTRY
Name:        Customer complaint reply
Used for:    Replying to unhappy customers on WhatsApp
Prompt:      Act as [business] support. Tone: warm, calm, brief.
             Follow the examples below exactly.
             Examples: [ex1] [ex2]
             Complaint: [paste]
             Rules: under 100 words, apologise once, give one next step.
Tested on:   5 real complaints, average score 4.4 / 5
Last update: [date]
Notes:       Fails when complaint contains legal threats: escalate.
mistakes: Giving examples that are all identical
Skipping your own review after self-critique

quiz.q: What is few-shot prompting?
quiz.a: Giving the AI a few examples of the output you want.

quiz.q: Name three useful constraints.
quiz.a: For example length, tone, required sections or banned words.

quiz.q: What does a self-critique prompt do?
quiz.a: Has the AI score and improve its own draft against criteria.

quiz.q: Why run a prompt several times?
quiz.a: To check it gives consistent results.

quiz.q: What goes into a prompt playbook entry?
quiz.a: Name, use, prompt, test results, date and notes.

A rule that limits the answer.
Asking the AI to review its own work.
A saved collection of tested prompts.

title: Prompt chains and brand voice

objectives: Break large tasks into prompt chains
Create a brand voice guide the AI can follow
Build reusable prompt templates with variables
Produce content in a consistent voice across several formats
content.intro: One giant prompt rarely gives a great result. Professionals split work into a chain of smaller steps, each with its own check. Today you learn chains, and you teach the AI the voice of a brand so that everything it writes sounds like the same trustworthy business.

concepts.heading: What a prompt chain is
concepts.text: A prompt chain passes the output of one step into the next: research, then outline, then draft, then edit, then final polish. Each step has a narrow job, so each result is easier to check and to fix. If the draft is weak you can rerun only that step instead of starting over. Chains also make it possible to save time by reusing the early steps for several products or campaigns.
points: Output of one step becomes input of the next
Narrow jobs are easier to check

concepts.heading: Brand voice guide
concepts.text: A brand voice guide tells the AI how the business speaks. It states who the customers are, three words that describe the tone and three that do not, words and phrases to use or avoid, and five real sample sentences. Paste the guide at the start of any writing task. The best guides are written from real messages the business has already sent, because AI copies what it sees.
points: Pasted at the start of every task

concepts.heading: Templates with variables
concepts.text: Turn successful chains into templates with variables in square brackets such as [product], [audience] and [offer]. A template lets you or a teammate produce a full piece of content in minutes by filling the brackets. Store templates in a shared document with a short name and instructions. Update them when you learn something better, and note the date of the last change.

concepts.heading: Consistency across formats
concepts.text: The same message needs different shapes on different channels: a long email, a short WhatsApp message, a caption with hashtags, a poster headline. Ask the AI to adapt one approved core message to each format instead of writing each from scratch, so facts and tone stay consistent. Always check that prices, dates and contact details match in every version.
points: Check prices and dates in every version

steps: Collect five real messages or posts from a business (yours, a friend's or a local shop) and underline what makes them sound like that business
Write the brand voice guide using the template
Build a four-step chain: research, outline, draft, edit and run it for one topic
Save the chain as a template with [variables]
Use one core message to produce an email, a WhatsApp message, a caption and a poster headline
Compare outputs against the guide and fix anything that does not sound right
content.lab: Create a brand voice guide for a business (real client or friend). Test with 3 content types.

examples.label: Voice prompt
examples.text: Use the brand voice guide below for everything you write. [paste guide]. First confirm in two sentences how you will write, then wait for my request.

examples.label: Chain step
examples.text: Using the outline above, write the first draft in the brand voice. Do not add facts that are not in the outline.

content.code:
CONTENT CHAIN
1 RESEARCH  Act as a market researcher for [business, place]. List 10 customer pain points.
2 OUTLINE   Using those pain points, propose 3 content ideas with a hook each.
3 DRAFT     Write the chosen idea in the brand voice: [paste guide].
4 EDIT      Review the draft against: one idea, clear hook, local relevance, one call to action.
            Score each 1-5 and rewrite where below 4.
5 ADAPT     Convert the final text into: email, WhatsApp message, caption, poster headline.
mistakes: Writing one huge prompt for everything
A voice guide invented instead of based on real messages
Never saving the chains that work

quiz.q: What is a prompt chain?
quiz.a: A series of steps where each output feeds the next.

quiz.q: Why is chaining useful?
quiz.a: Each step is smaller, easier to check and easy to rerun.

quiz.q: What goes in a brand voice guide?
quiz.a: Audience, tone words, vocabulary and sample sentences.

quiz.q: Why use variables in templates?
quiz.a: So the template can be reused quickly for different cases.

quiz.q: What must you check across formats?
quiz.a: Prices, dates, contacts and tone.

takeaways: Voice guides come from real samples

glossary.meaning: A sequence of connected prompts.
The consistent way a business sounds.
A reusable structure with blanks.
The main idea that every format repeats.

title: Research and strategy with AI

objectives: Run a structured market and competitor research workflow
Create customer personas based on evidence
Verify AI research with real sources and real customers
Write a two-page strategy brief
content.intro: Good content and good automation both start with understanding customers. AI can speed up research dramatically, but it can also give you confident nonsense about your market. Today you use AI to draft research and then you do the human work of checking it against reality.

concepts.heading: A research workflow
concepts.text: Start by writing the research question precisely: who is the customer, what are you trying to decide, and what place and time do you care about. Ask AI for a first map of the market: customer groups, needs, competitors, prices and trends. Treat this as a list of hypotheses, not facts. Then check the most important ones through real sources: competitor websites and pages, price lists, local observation and customer conversations.

concepts.heading: Competitor analysis
concepts.text: List three to five competitors, including informal ones such as the shop down the road or a popular online seller. For each note what they sell, their prices, how they communicate, what customers praise or complain about and what they do not offer. Ask AI to organise your notes into a comparison table and to highlight gaps. The gaps are your opportunities.

concepts.heading: Personas from evidence
concepts.text: A persona is a short description of a typical customer: who they are, their goals, worries, where they spend time and how they decide. Build personas from real interviews and observations, then ask AI to polish them. Personas invented from imagination lead to stereotypes. Give each persona a name, a one-sentence need and the exact words they use to describe their problem.

concepts.heading: The strategy brief
concepts.text: Summarise everything in a two-page brief: the audience, their top needs, your offer, how you are different, three content themes and three measures of success. Ask AI to draft it from your verified notes and mark anything unverified. A short evidence-based brief guides every later decision and protects you from chasing every new idea.
points: Audience, needs, offer, difference, themes, measures

steps: Write your research question and the decision it supports
Ask AI for a market map and list the five claims that matter most
Verify at least three claims using real sources and mark each as confirmed, wrong or unknown
Build a competitor table for four competitors from your own observation
Interview two real people for ten minutes and write down their exact words
Produce a two-page strategy brief with two personas and mark unverified items
content.lab: Produce a 2-page strategy brief: audience, offer, 3 content pillars, 5 competitors reviewed.

examples.label: Research prompt
examples.text: Act as a market researcher. I want to decide [decision] for a [business] in [place]. List customer groups, needs, typical competitors and price ranges, and mark which claims I must verify.

examples.label: Persona prompt
examples.text: Turn these interview notes into a one-paragraph persona with name, goal, worries and the exact phrases they used: [notes]

STRATEGY BRIEF (2 pages)
Audience:        [who] - top 3 needs: 1 .. 2 .. 3 ..   (confirmed by 2 interviews)
Persona 1:       [name], [age/role] - goal, worries, exact words: "[quote]"
Offer:           [what we sell and the price range]
Competitors:     [A] [B] [C]  - gaps we can fill: ..
How we differ:   [one sentence]
Content themes:  1 .. 2 .. 3 ..
Success measures: [reach / enquiries / sales target]
Unverified items: [list anything not yet checked]

Inventing personas without talking to anyone
Writing a long brief nobody reads

quiz.q: Why treat AI research as hypotheses?
quiz.a: It can be wrong or outdated and must be verified.

quiz.q: What should a competitor table compare?
quiz.a: Offer, price, communication, complaints and gaps.

quiz.q: What is a persona?
quiz.a: A short description of a typical customer.

quiz.q: Why interview real customers?
quiz.a: They reveal real needs and words that AI cannot know.

quiz.q: How long should a strategy brief be?
quiz.a: About two pages.

glossary.meaning: An idea that still needs checking.
A typical customer profile.
A business that serves the same customers.
What makes you different.

title: Visual and video content

objectives: Write effective image prompts for consistent brand visuals
Design carousels, posters and thumbnails in Canva
Produce a short video from script to captions
Follow ethics and licence rules for AI visuals
content.intro: Visuals decide whether people stop scrolling. Today you create a matching set of designs and a short video for one brand, using AI for ideas and drafts and your own judgement for quality, honesty and style.

concepts.heading: Visual consistency
concepts.text: A brand looks professional when colours, fonts, image style and layout repeat. Choose two or three brand colours, two fonts and an image style such as bright realistic photos or flat illustrations, and write them in your brand guide. Add the style to every image prompt: 'warm natural light, realistic photo, green and yellow palette'. Save good prompts so that future images match.
points: Put the style in every image prompt
Save prompts that match your brand

concepts.heading: Carousels, posters and thumbnails
concepts.text: A carousel tells a story across several slides: a hook slide, three to five value slides, and a final call to action. Posters need one message and clear hierarchy. Thumbnails need a big readable phrase and a strong image. Use Canva templates as a starting point, replace the content with your own and check readability on a phone-sized screen. If the text is hard to read at thumbnail size, it is too small.
points: Hook, value slides, call to action

concepts.heading: Short video workflow
concepts.text: A thirty to forty-five second video has a hook in the first three seconds, one useful idea and a call to action. Ask AI for a script and a shot list, then film on your phone in good light with steady hands and clear sound. Add captions because many people watch without sound. Edit in a simple tool such as CapCut, keep cuts quick and end with your contact or next step.
points: Hook, one idea, call to action

concepts.heading: Ethics, licences and honesty
concepts.text: Do not copy the style of a living artist or use a brand's logos without permission. Check licences for music and stock images. Do not create realistic images of real people doing things they did not do. If an image is AI-generated and could be mistaken for a real photo of your product, do not use it to show what the product looks like: customers must get what they see.
points: No fake images of real people

steps: Write the visual brand sheet: colours, fonts, image style and three example prompts
Generate a set of five images that match the style and select the best three
Design a seven-slide carousel in Canva with hook, value slides and call to action
Design a poster and a thumbnail from the same message
Write a 35-second script and shot list, film it, add captions and export
Review all pieces against the brand sheet and the ethics checklist
content.lab: Make 1 carousel, 1 poster and 1 short video (30-45 seconds) for the same brand.

examples.text: A friendly tailor in a bright Kenyan shop holding a measuring tape, warm natural light, realistic photo, green and yellow palette, no text.

examples.label: Script prompt
examples.text: Write a 35-second video script with a hook in the first 3 seconds, one useful tip and a call to action for [business]. Add a shot list.

Tiny text that cannot be read on a phone

title: Lab day: 2-Week Content Pack

objectives: Batch-produce a two-week content calendar with finished posts
Apply a quality checklist to every piece
Schedule or publish and plan measurement
Present your content pack
content.intro: Lab day for Week 1. You will produce a complete two-week content pack for one brand, using everything from the week: playbook, voice guide, research brief, visuals and chains. The goal is a package a real business could start using on Monday.

concepts.heading: Planning the pack
concepts.text: Start from the strategy brief: three content themes, the audience and the measures of success. Plan fourteen days with a mix of educational posts, product posts, customer stories and offers. Decide the format for each day and the call to action. Put the calendar in a table with date, theme, format, caption, visual and status so it is easy to manage and to hand to a client.
points: Themes, mix, format, call to action

concepts.heading: Batching
concepts.text: Batching means doing the same type of task for many pieces in one session: write all captions first, then make all graphics, then film all videos. It is faster because you avoid switching between tasks. Use your chain templates and brand guide to keep the quality steady, and take short breaks so your judgement stays sharp. Save drafts in a shared folder with a clear naming scheme.

concepts.heading: Quality checklist
concepts.text: Before anything is published check: facts and prices correct, spelling and names correct, tone matches the voice guide, visual matches the brand sheet, one clear call to action, no private data and no claims you cannot prove. Ask a second person to check. A simple checklist stops most embarrassing mistakes.
points: Facts, spelling, tone, visual, call to action
No private data or unproven claims

concepts.heading: Measuring and learning
concepts.text: Decide in advance how you will measure success: reach, saves, replies, enquiries or sales. After two weeks look at which themes and formats performed best and do more of those. Write down what you learned and update your playbook and brand guide. Content improves only through this loop of publishing, measuring and adjusting.

steps: Review your strategy brief and write the three themes and the success measures
Build the 14-day calendar table with date, theme, format, caption, visual and status
Batch all captions, then all graphics, then the videos
Run the quality checklist on every piece and fix errors
Swap packs with a partner for a second check using the checklist
Present your pack in two minutes: audience, themes, three best pieces and how you will measure

title: Automation thinking

objectives: Explain triggers, actions, filters and data mapping
Spot good automation opportunities with the 'do it three times' rule
Build a simple form-to-sheet-to-email automation
Think about reliability, errors and security
content.intro: Automation means that work happens by itself when something occurs: a form is filled, an email arrives, a time is reached. Combined with AI, it can read, decide and write as part of the chain. Today you learn the building blocks and make your first working automation.

concepts.heading: The building blocks
concepts.text: Every automation has a trigger that starts it, one or more actions that do things, and often filters or conditions that decide whether to continue. Data flows between steps: the name typed in a form becomes a cell in a sheet and a greeting in an email. Matching a piece of data from one step to a field in the next is called mapping. Tools such as Make, n8n and Zapier let you build these chains visually by connecting boxes.

concepts.heading: Finding good opportunities
concepts.text: Use the 'do it three times' rule: if you do the same task three times, consider automating it. The best candidates are frequent, rule-based and low-risk: sending confirmation emails, saving form responses, copying data between tools, weekly reports, reminders and sorting messages. Poor candidates are rare tasks, tasks needing deep judgement, or those with serious consequences if wrong. Estimate the time saved per week to decide whether it is worth building.

concepts.heading: Process mapping before building
concepts.text: Never start by clicking in the tool. Draw the current process on paper: who starts it, what information arrives, what decisions are made, what is produced and who is told. Mark each step as manual, decision or automatable. Automating a messy process only makes the mess faster, so remove unnecessary steps first. Then plan the data fields you will need.

concepts.heading: Reliability, errors and security
concepts.text: Automations fail: a form field is empty, a service is down, a limit is reached. Plan for it by adding error notifications, default values and a way to see what ran and when. Give each connection the minimum access it needs and never share your login with a tool you do not trust. Test with sample data, not live customer data, and keep a note of what each automation does and who owns it.
points: Test with sample data; document owners

steps: Choose a real repetitive task and draw its current process on paper
Mark each step manual, decision or automatable and estimate weekly time
Create a Google Form and linked Sheet with five fields
Build an automation: new form response -> add row -> send confirmation email with data mapped from the form
Test with five sample entries including an empty field and note what breaks
Add an error notification and write a three-line description of the automation
content.lab: Process-map a real workflow on paper, then build a simple automation (form -> sheet -> email).

examples.label: Process map

title: AI inside automations

objectives: Add an AI step with a prompt template to an automation
Use AI to classify, summarise and draft inside a workflow
Design human-in-the-loop approvals
Test with realistic sample data
content.intro: Plain automations follow fixed rules. When you add an AI step, the workflow can read free text, understand it and write a reply. This opens many possibilities but also brings risks, so today we also add a human check. You will build a customer enquiry workflow that classifies, drafts and waits for approval.

concepts.heading: Where the AI step goes
concepts.text: An AI step takes input from earlier in the chain, such as the customer's message, applies a prompt template and produces output that later steps use. Typical jobs are: classify a message (question, complaint, order), extract details (product, quantity, date), summarise a long text, and draft a reply. In your automation tool you add an AI or HTTP step, put the prompt in, and map the message into it.

concepts.heading: Writing prompts for workflows
concepts.text: A workflow prompt must work without you watching. State the task, the allowed categories, the exact output format and what to do when unsure. For example: 'Classify into exactly one of: order, question, complaint, other. Reply with only the word.' Fixed outputs let later steps route correctly. Test with many sample messages including strange ones, and tell the AI to answer 'other' rather than guess.
points: Say what to do when unsure

concepts.heading: Human in the loop
concepts.text: Do not let AI send important messages unchecked. Insert an approval step: the draft is sent to a person by email or chat with approve and reject choices, and only approved drafts are sent. Over time, for low-risk categories and when accuracy is proven, you can reduce approvals. Always keep a human check for money, complaints, health or legal topics.
points: Reduce checks only when proven safe

concepts.heading: Testing and monitoring
concepts.text: Build a test set of twenty realistic messages, including spelling errors, mixed languages, angry customers, spam and unclear requests. Run them all and check each result. Record the accuracy of the classification and note failures. After launch look at a sample of real cases every week. AI behaviour changes with prompts and models, so keep testing.

steps: Write 20 sample customer messages with different types, mistakes and tones
Write the classification prompt with fixed categories and an 'other' fallback
Build the workflow: form or email trigger -> AI classify -> router by category
For 'question' and 'order' categories add an AI draft reply step using your brand voice guide
Add an approval email to the manager with the draft; send the reply only after approval
Run all 20 samples, record accuracy and fix the prompt until at least 17 are correct
content.lab: Build: new customer form -> AI classifies and drafts reply -> manager approves -> email sent.

examples.label: Classifier prompt
examples.text: Classify the message into exactly one of: order, question, complaint, other. If unsure choose other. Reply with only the word. Message: {{message}}

examples.label: Draft prompt
examples.text: Using the brand voice guide, draft a reply under 80 words to this message: {{message}}. Do not invent prices or dates. If information is missing, ask for it.

2 AI classify -> order | question | complaint | other
3 Router      order -> step 4     question -> step 5     complaint -> manager     other -> log
4 AI extract  product, quantity, phone as JSON -> write to Sheet

Giving the AI invented prices or policies

quiz.a: Classify, extract, summarise or draft.

quiz.a: So the workflow can route reliably.

quiz.q: What is human in the loop?
quiz.a: A person approves before an action happens.

concepts.heading: Extracting data from text and files
concepts.text: AI can read an email, an order message or a text from a PDF and return clean fields such as name, date, product and amount. For scanned files use text recognition first, and check a sample of results by hand.

concepts.heading: Generating documents

content.intro: Many Kenyan businesses sell and serve customers through WhatsApp, calls and social media. Automation can make responses faster, but messaging people carries legal and ethical duties. Today you design customer workflows that are helpful, respectful and legal.

concepts.heading: Customer messaging workflows
concepts.text: A common workflow: a customer enquires, the system records the lead, sends an instant acknowledgement, routes the message to the right person, and follows up after a set time if there is no reply. Each message type has a template. Keep a single sheet or CRM where every lead, status and next action is recorded so nothing is forgotten.

concepts.heading: WhatsApp Business and the Cloud API
concepts.text: WhatsApp Business app offers a profile, catalogue, labels, quick replies and away messages, which is enough for many small businesses. For larger volumes the Cloud API lets software send and receive messages through a webhook, but business-initiated messages must use approved templates and respect the platform's rules. Learn the current policies before building anything, because they change.
points: Business app: catalogue, labels, quick replies
Cloud API: webhooks and approved templates

concepts.heading: Consent, privacy and opt-out
concepts.text: Only message people who have agreed to hear from you. Collect consent clearly at the point of data collection, say what you will send and how often, and make it easy to stop: a reply such as STOP must be honoured immediately. Store only the data you need, protect it, and do not share customer numbers. Kenya's Data Protection Act expects lawful, transparent handling of personal data.
points: Collect and keep only what you need

concepts.heading: Tone and timing
concepts.text: Automated messages should feel helpful, not pushy. Send during reasonable hours, keep messages short, use the customer's name and make the next step obvious. Limit follow-ups: one reminder after two days is polite, five in a week is spam. Always give a way to reach a human. Review replies regularly and learn from complaints.

objectives: Clean and analyse a business dataset with AI help

content.intro: Businesses sit on data they never look at: sales records, orders, expenses, customer lists. AI makes analysis much more accessible, but it can also make confident arithmetic mistakes. Today you analyse a real dataset the right way: AI to explore, spreadsheets to calculate, and you to decide.

concepts.heading: Cleaning data first
concepts.text: Most analysis time goes on cleaning. Look for blank cells, duplicates, inconsistent spellings (Nairobi, nairobi, NBO), dates in different formats and numbers stored as text. Ask AI how to fix each problem in your spreadsheet tool and work on a copy of the original. Record every cleaning step so the analysis can be repeated and explained to someone else.
points: Blanks, duplicates, spellings, dates, number formats

concepts.heading: Asking good analysis questions
concepts.text: Begin with business questions: which products sell best, which days are busiest, which customers return, where do costs rise? Describe the columns to the AI and ask it to suggest analyses, then ask for the spreadsheet formulas or pivot table steps to produce them. This keeps the arithmetic inside the spreadsheet where it is exact and visible, and uses AI for guidance and explanation.

concepts.heading: Charts and insights
concepts.text: Choose the chart to match the message: a line for change over time, bars for comparing groups, a pie only for a few parts of a whole. Give every chart a clear title that states the insight, such as 'Saturday sales are 40% higher than weekdays'. Ask AI to describe what a chart shows in plain language and then check the description against the numbers.
points: Line for time, bars for groups

concepts.heading: From insight to recommendation
concepts.text: An insight is only useful if it leads to an action. For each finding ask: so what, and what should we do? Write three recommendations, each with the evidence, the expected benefit and a simple way to test it. Be honest about limits: a small dataset or a short time period may not show the whole truth. Correlation does not prove cause.

objectives: Build a live dashboard from a Google Sheet

content.intro: A dashboard is a one-page view of how a business is doing. Done well, it replaces long meetings and guesswork. Today you build one with Looker Studio or similar, choose measures that actually drive decisions, and write the short summary that tells people what to do.

concepts.heading: Choosing KPIs
concepts.text: A KPI, or key performance indicator, is a number that shows progress toward a goal. Choose few and make them meaningful: for a shop perhaps weekly revenue, number of orders, repeat customers, and gross margin; for a service business enquiries, conversion rate and average response time. Avoid vanity numbers that look impressive but change no decision. For each KPI write its definition, source and target.

concepts.heading: Building the dashboard
concepts.text: Connect the sheet as a data source, then add scorecards for the main KPIs, a trend chart over time, a breakdown by product or channel and a table of recent rows. Add date filters so users can change the period. Keep the layout clean with the most important number at the top left, consistent colours and readable labels. Test it on a phone because many owners view it there.

concepts.heading: The executive summary
concepts.text: Managers rarely read details. Write five or six sentences: what happened, why it probably happened, what it means and what you recommend. Lead with the most important point. Use AI to tighten your draft, but supply the numbers yourself and check that every figure matches the dashboard. A summary that is clear and honest earns trust.

concepts.heading: Sharing safely
concepts.text: Dashboards can reveal sensitive business or customer data. Share with named people, not with anyone who has the link, remove personal information such as phone numbers, and give view-only access unless someone needs to edit. Review who has access regularly and remove people who have left. Keep the source sheet more restricted than the dashboard.

concepts.heading: Choosing a niche
concepts.text: Beginners try to serve everyone and convince no one. Choose a specific group and a specific problem: for example 'WhatsApp customer reply systems for small salons' or 'monthly social content for restaurants'. A niche makes your message clear, lets you reuse templates and builds your reputation. Pick one where you understand the customers or can learn quickly, and where people already spend money.

concepts.heading: Packages and pricing
concepts.text: Package your work into three clear offers: a starter, a standard and a premium, each with defined deliverables, timeline and revisions. concepts.heading: Proposals and portfolio

A portfolio page shows two or three case studies with the problem, what you did and the result, ideally with a short quote from a client. If you have no clients yet, do a small free pilot for a friendly business and document it honestly.

concepts.heading: Finding clients respectfully
concepts.text: Start with people you know and local businesses you can visit. Offer to solve one small visible problem. On platforms such as Upwork, Fiverr and LinkedIn write a clear profile and send personalised proposals that quote the client's own words from the job post; copy-paste proposals are ignored. Follow up once or twice, politely. Never send unsolicited bulk messages: it is rude and often illegal.

content.intro: Lab day for Week 3. You will practise the human side of client work: asking good questions, explaining value, handling doubts and delivering a professional experience. Technical skill gets you the work; communication keeps the client.

concepts.heading: The discovery call
concepts.text: Before offering anything, learn the client's situation. Ask what they do now, what frustrates them, how much time or money the problem costs, what they have tried and what a good result would look like. Listen more than you talk and write down their exact words. At the end, summarise what you heard and ask permission to send a proposal. Clients buy when they feel understood.
points: Ask about situation, pain, cost, goal

concepts.heading: Handling objections
concepts.text: Common objections are 'it is too expensive', 'I will think about it', 'we tried that before' and 'my customers will not like AI'. Treat each as a request for more information. Ask what concerns them, answer honestly, offer a smaller start such as a pilot, and never pressure. Sometimes the right answer is 'this is not the right time', and that is fine.

concepts.heading: Delivering professionally
concepts.text: Agree scope, price, timeline and revisions in writing before starting. Keep the client updated with short progress messages. Deliver on time with a clear handover: files, how-to and a short training. Send a clear invoice with payment details and due date. Ask for feedback and a testimonial after delivery, and offer a simple follow-up plan.

concepts.heading: The 90-second pitch
concepts.text: A pitch has four parts: the problem your client has, your solution in one sentence, proof that you can deliver and a clear next step. Practise aloud until you can say it naturally without reading. Adjust it for each audience: a restaurant owner cares about customers and time, a manager about cost and risk. Simple words and calm confidence win.

title: Discovery and project plan

objectives: Choose a client and agree a clear project brief
Write a two-page project plan with scope, timeline and measures

content.intro: The capstone is your professional debut: you deliver a complete AI solution for a real or simulated client. Today you do what every good project starts with, which is understanding the client and agreeing exactly what will be delivered. Careful planning now prevents confusion later.

concepts.heading: Choosing the right client and project
concepts.text: Choose a client you can reach during the week and a problem that fits ten working days: a content system, an automation, or a customer assistant. A small shop, a school office, a church group or a friend's online business all work. If you cannot find a client, your trainer will provide a simulated brief with sample documents. Agree who will give feedback and when, because a client who disappears can sink a project.

concepts.heading: The project brief
concepts.text: Write the brief with the client: the problem in their own words, who the users are, what a successful result looks like, what you will deliver and what is out of scope. Add the tools that will be used and what information or access you need from the client. Ask them to read it and say 'yes, this is what I want'. Changes later should be agreed in writing.
points: Problem, users, success, deliverables, out of scope

concepts.heading: Plan, timeline and measures
concepts.text: Break the work into milestones: discovery done, first version, testing, handover. Give each a date and a measurable result, such as 'assistant answers 22 of 25 test questions correctly' or 'weekly report arrives automatically every Monday'. Allow time for testing and for the client's feedback. Add a buffer of one or two days because something always takes longer.

concepts.heading: Risks and data protection
concepts.text: List what could go wrong: the client is slow to respond, the data is messy, the AI makes mistakes, a tool changes or fails. For each risk write how you will reduce it. Check the data: use only what the client is allowed to share, remove personal details where possible, tell the client how information will be stored and who will see it, and delete test data at the end.
points: List risks with a response each
Delete test data at the end

title: Build sprint 1

objectives: Prioritise a minimum viable solution
Build the core workflow or content system
Use daily stand-ups and mentor checkpoints

content.intro: Building day. Your job is to get the core of the solution working end to end, even if it is plain. A working simple version lets the client react to something real, which is far more valuable than a perfect plan. Keep communicating, keep notes and keep your scope under control.

concepts.heading: Minimum viable solution
concepts.text: List everything the client might want, then mark what is essential for the problem to be solved. Build only that first. For a content project it might be the brand voice guide, one tested chain and the first week of content. For an automation, the trigger, the main action and an error alert. For an assistant, the knowledge document, instructions and a first round of tests. Add extras only after the core works.

concepts.heading: Working in short cycles
concepts.text: Work in cycles of ninety minutes: build, test, note what changed. After each cycle take a short break and decide the next step. Use a simple board with three columns, to do, doing and done, and move cards as you go. If a task is stuck for more than fifteen minutes ask a classmate or mentor; this is normal and not a weakness.
points: Ask for help after fifteen minutes

concepts.heading: Stand-ups and mentor checkpoints
concepts.text: Start the day with a five-minute stand-up with your partner or mentor: what I finished, what I am doing today, what is blocking me. At mid-day show your work in progress to a mentor and invite honest questions. Short regular check-ins reveal problems early, when they are cheap to fix.

concepts.heading: Documenting as you go
concepts.text: Do not leave documentation until the end. Keep a build log with what you did, which prompts and settings you used, what failed and why. Save every important prompt, template and automation setting in a folder. This log becomes your how-to and your case study, and it saves you if something breaks or if you need to explain your choices.
points: Log becomes how-to and case study

title: Build sprint 2

objectives: Test with realistic inputs and edge cases
Handle errors and write clear user instructions
Complete the solution and get client feedback
Run a safety and privacy check
content.intro: Today you move from 'it works on my examples' to 'it works for real people'. You will test harder, fix weaknesses, write instructions that a non-expert can follow and collect honest client feedback.

concepts.heading: Testing with real inputs
concepts.text: Use real or realistic inputs from the client: typical, unusual, wrong and rude ones. Write down every test and result in a table. Look for patterns in failures rather than fixing each one blindly. Re-test everything after any change to a prompt or setting because small edits can change behaviour. Aim for a pass mark you agreed with the client in the plan.

concepts.heading: Edge cases and error handling
concepts.text: Edge cases are the odd situations: empty fields, very long messages, unexpected languages, duplicate requests, and times when a service is unavailable. Decide what should happen in each: a polite message, a default value, a notification to a human or a safe stop. A solution that fails gracefully is more valuable than one that is perfect only when everything goes right.
points: Empty, long, odd, duplicate, service down

concepts.heading: User instructions
concepts.text: Write for the person who will use the solution without you. Use short numbered steps and screenshots, plain words and a section called 'If something goes wrong'. Test the instructions by asking someone who has never seen the project to follow them. Wherever they hesitate, rewrite. Good instructions reduce support calls.

concepts.heading: Safety and privacy check
concepts.text: Before handover review: is personal data minimised and protected, are keys and passwords stored safely, are customers told when they talk to AI where appropriate, does a human check risky outputs, and could the system say something harmful or false? Fix gaps. Delete test data. Write down what the system cannot do so the client does not assume more than is true.

content.intro: Your capstone is only valuable if people can see it and understand it. Today you turn your work into evidence: a case study, a portfolio page and a professional handover. This is what you will show future clients and employers.

concepts.heading: Writing a case study
concepts.text: A case study tells the story of one project in four parts: the client and their problem, what you did, the results with numbers, and what you learned. Use the client's own words when you can. Include a screenshot or sample. Keep it to one page. Numbers such as hours saved, response time or pass rate convince far more than adjectives. Ask the client's permission before publishing and remove confidential details.

concepts.heading: Building a portfolio page
concepts.text: A portfolio page can be a simple Canva presentation, a Google Site or a single page document. Include a short introduction about who you help, two or three case studies, your service packages and how to contact you. Make it easy to read on a phone. Keep it honest: only include work you did, and label pilots and practice projects as such.

concepts.heading: The handover pack
concepts.text: Give the client a folder with: the finished solution, the user guide, the how-to for any automation, a list of accounts and settings (without passwords in plain text), the test results and a short training session. Agree who owns what and what support you provide afterwards, for example two weeks of free fixes and optional paid support. Clear handover prevents misunderstandings.

concepts.heading: Testimonials and next steps
concepts.text: Ask the client for a short testimonial: what problem you solved and what changed. Offer examples of what to include so it is easy to write, but never write it for them. Ask whether they know anyone else who could benefit. Offer a simple next step such as a monthly support plan or an improvement project. Thank them sincerely.

title: Demo Day and graduation

objectives: Deliver a ten-minute demo with confidence
Answer questions from business guests honestly
Give and receive feedback with a scorecard

content.intro: Demo Day brings together learners, families and local business owners. You will show a real solution you built for a real problem. Be proud of what you made, honest about its limits and curious about the questions. Many careers and clients start from a good demo.

concepts.heading: Delivering the demo
concepts.text: Check your equipment early and have your backup ready. Structure ten minutes like this: two minutes on the client and the problem, four minutes showing the solution working, two minutes on results with numbers, and two minutes on lessons and next steps. Speak slowly, face the audience and show the real thing. If something fails, switch to the backup calmly and explain what should have happened.

concepts.heading: Answering questions
concepts.text: Listen to the whole question, pause and answer briefly and honestly. Expect questions about cost, accuracy, safety, data privacy and 'will it replace my staff?'. Prepare short truthful answers. If you do not know, say 'I do not know yet, and here is how I would find out'. Never invent facts to sound clever. Thank the person for asking.

concepts.heading: Scorecards and feedback
concepts.text: Use a simple scorecard to rate each demo from one to five on: problem clarity, quality of solution, evidence and results, safety and responsibility, and communication, with one comment each. Give feedback as strength, question and suggestion. When receiving feedback, listen, write it down and decide later what to change. Feedback is how professionals improve.

concepts.heading: Your next 90 days
concepts.text: Decide what you will do next: find your first paying client, join a team, continue to the Advanced path, or start your own small service. Write three goals and one weekly habit, such as one outreach message per day or one new case study per month. Tell someone your plan and meet them in a month to review. Keep a record of your results.
points: Three goals and one weekly habit
